n:Ikililou Dhoinine: Ikililou Dhoinine, based in Moroni, is a former president of the Comoros. A Comorian parliamentary commission of inquiry into the economic citizenship programme, which sold Comorian nationality, reported in December 2017 that, according to his own collaborators, he ordered that from January 2015 until the end of his term the programme's money no longer be paid into the Banque Centrale des Comores, and that he could not explain what became of it. It concluded he was suspected of embezzling public money, which is unproven.
n:Legislative Assembly of El Salvador: The Legislative Assembly is El Salvador's parliament, in San Salvador. One of its commissions investigated the debt the government took on during the COVID-19 pandemic and how it was spent, and summoned Nicolás Martínez, president of the Banco Central de Reserva, the country's central bank. Deputies asked whether releasing the banks' liquidity reserve was designed so banks could buy government Treasury paper; he said that was an autonomous decision of the banks. He resigned the day after appearing, with no reason given.
n:Majlisi Namoyandagon of the Majlisi Ol: The Majlisi Namoyandagon is the lower house of Tajikistan's parliament, in Dushanbe, and its role over the National Bank of Tajikistan is approval only. The Law on the National Bank of Tajikistan, No. 722 of 28 June 2011, signed by President Emomali Rahmon, provides in article 74(4) that the Chairman and his deputies are appointed and released by presidential decree, with the decrees submitted to the lower house for approval. Article 74(3) has the board's three independent members approved by the President, and article 74(6) has him set their pay.
n:Ministry of Economy and Foreign Trade: This ministry, in Damascus, sits over the Central Bank of Syria. Under the Basic Monetary Law No. 23 of 2002, issued on 17 March 2002 by President Bashar al-Assad, the bank's Monetary and Credit Council works within the state's general economic directions approved by the Council of Ministers. Article 8(3) lets the Minister suspend for up to seven days any Council decision he considers contrary to the state's interest, and refer a continuing disagreement to the Council of Ministers. Article 69 has the Governor appointed and removed by decree.
n:Ministry of Finance of Aruba: Aruba's finance ministry, in Oranjestad, shares control of the Centrale Bank van Aruba with the island's Governor. Under the Central Bank Ordinance (AB 1991 no. GT 32), as amended through AB 2014 no. 5, section 18 has the president and executive directors appointed by the Governor from a shortlist of three put up by the Supervisory Board. Section 23 has the Governor appoint the supervisory directors, whose chairman is the Government Commissioner; under section 27(1) that Commissioner supervises the bank for the country and acts on the Minister's instructions.
n:Ministry of Finance of Bermuda: Bermuda's finance ministry, in Hamilton, appoints and can instruct the Bermuda Monetary Authority. Under the Bermuda Monetary Authority Act 1969, section 21(2) lets the Minister give the Authority written general directions that appear to him necessary in the public interest, and the Authority must act in accordance with them. Section 4(1)(d) has eleven board members appointed by the Minister, section 4E(1) has him appoint the Chairman, and section 4E(6) lets him end the Chairman's appointment if satisfied he is unable or unfit. The arrangement is standing, with no end date.
n:Ministry of Finance of Solomon Islands: The finance ministry in Honiara draws its powers over the Central Bank of Solomon Islands from the Central Bank of Solomon Islands Act 2012. Section 37 lets the Minister, with Cabinet's approval, give the bank written directions on public-interest or policy-coordination grounds, but they must be published in the Gazette and laid before Parliament. Section 41(3) has the Minister appoint the other board directors after consulting the Governor. Section 44 allows removal before a term ends only for permanent incapacity or serious misconduct.
n:Ministry of Finance of Timor-Leste: Timor-Leste's finance ministry, in Dili, was named in findings by the country's Court of Accounts on the 2019 General State Account. The court found that 6.6 million US dollars of European Union budget support, held in three accounts at the Banco Central de Timor-Leste, was not booked as state revenue, understating 2019 revenue by that amount, and that the 2.3 million US dollars spent from those accounts was spent outside the state budget.
n:Ministry of Finance of Tonga: Tonga's finance ministry, in Nukuʻalofa, appoints most of the National Reserve Bank of Tonga's board. Under the National Reserve Bank of Tonga Act, Chapter 16.12, 2020 Revised Edition, section 10(1) has the Minister, with Cabinet's consent, appoint five directors and the Chairman and Deputy Chairman. Section 11(3) allows the Governor's removal only for permanent incapacity, serious misconduct or failure to perform his duties. Section 50(1) lets the Minister issue written directives with Cabinet's consent.
n:President of Tajikistan: The presidency, in Dushanbe, controls every seat on the board of the National Bank of Tajikistan, the country's central bank. Under the Law on the National Bank of Tajikistan, No. 722 of 28 June 2011, signed by President Emomali Rahmon, article 74(4) has the Chairman and his deputies appointed and released by presidential decree, with the decrees submitted to the lower house of parliament for approval. Article 74(3) has the board's three independent members approved by the President on the Chairman's proposal, and article 74(6) has him set their salaries.
n:Senate of Haiti: The Senate is the upper house of Haiti's parliament, in Port-au-Prince. Its Economy and Finance commission summoned Charles Castel, governor of the Banque de la République d'Haïti, the country's central bank, along with Ronald Baudin, Minister of Economy and Finance, to appear on Wednesday 1 June 2011. They were called to answer questions about new taxes of one dollar fifty US on each incoming or outgoing money transfer and five US cents a minute on incoming international calls.
n:Stichting Fondo Desaroyo Aruba: Stichting Fondo Desaroyo Aruba is a foundation based in Oranjestad. Aruba's General Audit Chamber, reviewing the country's annual accounts for 2001 to 2004, found that contributions paid for the foundation into an earmarked account held in the country's name at the Centrale Bank van Aruba were not accounted for completely, correctly and on time. Of a balance of 19.3 million Aruban florins at the end of 2000, only the 3 million paid in by Aruba appeared in the accounts.
